deep.reconstruction:
The page holds four equations in a spherical triangle. The sides are a, b, c and the opposite angles are A, B, C.

(1) cos(A/2)·cos((b−c)/2) = cos(a/2)·sin((B+C)/2)
(2) cos(A/2)·sin((b−c)/2) = sin(a/2)·sin((B−C)/2)
(3) sin(A/2)·cos((b+c)/2) = cos(a/2)·cos((B+C)/2)
(4) sin(A/2)·sin((b+c)/2) = sin(a/2)·cos((B−C)/2)

These are the four 'Gauss (Delambre, Mollweide) analogies' of spherical trigonometry. Each one links two sides, the included angle, and the three remaining parts.

The page gives only the results. The derivation is my reconstruction, and the previous folio (6r) supports it. On 6r Gauss manipulates sin(b+c) − cos A·sin(b+c) = (1−cos A)·sin(b+c) and sin(b−c) + sin(b−c)·cos A. These are exactly the combinations that arise when one starts from the cosine rule and the sine rule:
- cos a = cos b cos c + sin b sin c cos A
- sin B / sin b = sin C / sin c = sin A / sin a

One forms the sums and differences sin B ± sin C and cos B ± cos C, using expressions such as sin a·cos B = cos b sin c − sin b cos c cos A. Then one factors with half-angle identities. The factors 1 ∓ cos A become 2sin²(A/2) and 2cos²(A/2), and sin(b±c) splits into half-angle products. Squaring and adding pairs of the four equations recovers the half-angle formulas for a.

The next folio (7r) is a clean summary of spherical-trigonometry formulas, 'Trigonometria sphaerica', for right and oblique triangles. It includes Napier's analogies (its items 7 and 8). Those follow at once from the present four equations by division:
- (1)/(3) gives tan((B+C)/2) = cos((b−c)/2)·cot(A/2) / cos((b+c)/2)
- (2)/(4) gives tan((B−C)/2) = sin((b−c)/2)·cot(A/2) / sin((b+c)/2)

So this slip is a working note for that summary.

The pencil '37' lower centre is probably a later archival or page number. It is not part of the mathematics.
errors: None. All four equations are correct, in the standard form with the half-angle of the included angle on the left and the half-side a on the right.
In line 3 Gauss first wrote something like 'sin' or 'cos' and overwrote it to read cos(a/2). The final reading cos(a/2) is correct.

results.what: The four half-angle relations cos(A/2)cos((b−c)/2)=cos(a/2)sin((B+C)/2), cos(A/2)sin((b−c)/2)=sin(a/2)sin((B−C)/2), sin(A/2)cos((b+c)/2)=cos(a/2)cos((B+C)/2), sin(A/2)sin((b+c)/2)=sin(a/2)cos((B−C)/2) for a spherical triangle.
results.modern_name: Delambre's analogies / Gauss's formulas (Gauss–Delambre–Mollweide analogies) of spherical trigonometry
results.usually_credited_to: Delambre (1807, in Connaissance des Tems for 1809) and Mollweide (1808). Gauss published them independently in Theoria motus (1809, art. 54), and they are often called 'Gauss's formulas'.

deep.surprise_reason: These are exactly the formulas Gauss published in Theoria motus (1809), widely known as Gauss's analogies. The page is a working note restating them, apparently for the spherical-trigonometry summary on the next folio. It contains nothing beyond his published work.
